pathway_hypotheses.title: MTAP-associated methionine salvage vulnerability and 9p21 co-locus interaction
pathway_hypotheses.patient_specific_basis: MTAP RNA underexpression and DNA copy-number loss are reported. CDKN2A RNA underexpression and a low-confidence CDKN2B copy-number-loss call raise the possibility of a broader 9p21 event, but RNA underexpression, heterozygous copy loss, homozygous deletion, protein loss, and complete metabolic loss are not equivalent. The CDKN2B RNA annotation is internally discordant.
simplified_pathway: MTAP normally participates in methylthioadenosine salvage and methionine/adenine recycling.
Complete MTAP loss can permit methylthioadenosine accumulation.
That metabolic state may create a context-dependent dependency within the PRMT5-associated methylation pathway.
A neighboring 9p21 deletion can also involve CDKN2A or CDKN2B and thereby couple metabolic alteration to cell-cycle dysregulation.
This case does not yet establish homozygous MTAP deletion, absent MTAP protein, methylthioadenosine accumulation, or the proposed dependency.
potential_vulnerabilities: Investigational MTAP-null metabolic dependencies if complete functional MTAP loss is confirmed
Potential PRMT5-pathway dependency associated with methylthioadenosine accumulation
Potential interaction between a 9p21 co-deletion and cell-cycle checkpoint loss
potential_bypass_or_escape_routes: Residual MTAP expression from a retained allele or non-tumor cells
Failure to accumulate methylthioadenosine despite RNA or copy-number reduction
Alternative methionine salvage or methyl-donor homeostasis
Cell-cycle progression driven independently of CDKN2A or CDKN2B status
potential_combination_or_recombination_p: Mechanistic and investigational hypothesis: if complete MTAP loss and RB-dependent cell-cycle dysregulation are both confirmed, combined study of the metabolic dependency and cell-cycle control may be biologically plausible; this is not a treatment recommendation.

Mechanistic and investigational hypothesis: pharmacodynamic measurement of methylthioadenosine and PRMT5-associated methylation could be paired with genomic and protein confirmation to distinguish true metabolic dependency from a passenger 9p21 loss.

CDKN2A and CDKN2B absolute copy number

pathway_hypotheses.title: CDKN2A/CDKN2B–RB cell-cycle checkpoint dysregulation
pathway_hypotheses.patient_specific_basis: CDKN2A is underexpressed at the RNA level. CDKN2B has a low-confidence DNA copy-number-loss call, but its RNA annotation is contradictory. MTAP alteration may reflect a neighboring 9p21 event. None of these observations alone proves loss of p16INK4A or p15INK4B protein or an intact downstream RB dependency.
simplified_pathway: p16INK4A and p15INK4B normally restrain CDK4/6-mediated cell-cycle entry.
Reduced inhibitor function may permit RB phosphorylation and progression from G1 to S phase.
A genomic 9p21 deletion could affect CDKN2A, CDKN2B, and MTAP together.
RNA underexpression does not establish DNA deletion or protein loss.
If RB1 is absent or nonfunctional, the expected downstream dependency may not be present.
potential_vulnerabilities: RB-dependent cell-cycle control if p16INK4A or p15INK4B function is truly lost
Sarcoma clinical-trial hypotheses requiring a validated CDK-pathway alteration
potential_bypass_or_escape_routes: Cyclin or CDK pathway activation independent of CDKN2A/CDKN2B
Parallel mitogenic signaling, potentially including activated AKT signaling if independently confirmed
potential_combination_or_recombination_p: Mechanistic and investigational hypothesis: evaluate whether confirmed 9p21 loss and confirmed AKT-pathway activation represent parallel cell-cycle and survival dependencies; this is not a treatment recommendation.
Mechanistic and investigational hypothesis: integrate DNA copy number, p16/p15 protein, RB1 status, and RB phosphorylation before assigning a functional cell-cycle phenotype.

pathway_hypotheses.title: Unconfirmed CHEK2–TP53 DNA-damage checkpoint impairment
pathway_hypotheses.patient_specific_basis: CHEK2 c.846+4_846+7del is reported as a splice-region loss-of-function variant, but transcript-specific splice effect, allele status, and somatic-versus-germline origin remain unresolved. A TP53 splice-region call is also present, but it is low confidence and lacks an exact variant. Their coexistence could affect checkpoint signaling only if both are validated.
simplified_pathway: DNA damage can activate checkpoint signaling that includes CHEK2.
CHEK2 can contribute to cell-cycle arrest, repair coordination, and apoptosis through downstream effectors including p53.
A functionally damaging CHEK2 event may weaken this checkpoint.
A concurrent functional TP53 alteration could further reduce arrest or apoptosis.
The current evidence does not establish biallelic CHEK2 loss, TP53 loss, homologous-recombination deficiency, or sensitivity to a DNA-damage-directed strategy.
potential_vulnerabilities: Investigational checkpoint or DNA-damage-response dependencies only after functional validation
Potentially altered response to genotoxic stress, without a predictable direction from this record alone
potential_bypass_or_escape_routes: Retention of a functional CHEK2 allele
Splice variant that preserves sufficient CHEK2 function
Restoration or selection of alternate DNA repair pathways
potential_combination_or_recombination_p: Mechanistic and investigational hypothesis: assess whether validated CHEK2 loss and validated TP53 dysfunction jointly suppress checkpoint-mediated arrest or apoptosis; this is not a treatment recommendation.
Recombination-related hypothesis: evaluate homologous-recombination function independently rather than inferring it from CHEK2 alone.
